title: UAE Warns Workers: Change Jobs Wrong, Face a One-Year Permit Ban
excerpt: The Ministry of Human Resources clarifies post-contract job mobility rules, with strict penalties for probation violations and unauthorized absences.
body:
The United Arab Emirates has issued a fresh warning to its millions of expatriate workers: change jobs the wrong way and face a one-year ban on new work permits.

The Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation (MOHRE) published updated guidance this week clarifying when employees can legally move to a new employer after their contract ends — and, critically, when they cannot. Under Federal Decree Law No. 33 of 2021, workers who terminate employment during their probation period, are subject to a valid work abandonment report, or have permits cancelled at fictitious establishments will be barred from obtaining a new work permit for twelve months.

The Fine Print:

The clarification comes as the UAE continues to modernize its labour market. Since 2022, the old No Objection Certificate (NOC) requirement has been largely eliminated for private-sector workers. Employees can now switch employers freely after serving proper notice — typically 30 to 90 days depending on the contract. But the freedom is not absolute. Workers who walk off the job, skip their notice period, or are found to be employed at shell companies still face the full force of the ban.

The rules also specify that high-skill professionals and those on family-sponsored visas are exempt from most ban provisions, creating a two-tier system that disproportionately affects blue-collar and mid-level workers — the very demographic where Indian nationals are heavily represented.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora:

The UAE is home to an estimated 3.5 million Indians, making them the largest expatriate community in the country. From construction labourers in Abu Dhabi to IT professionals in Dubai's free zones, Indian workers are deeply embedded in the Emirates economy. A one-year permit ban can be devastating — it effectively means deportation or living without legal work status, with no recourse to earn a livelihood.

Labour rights advocates have long flagged the power imbalance these rules create. 'Workers often leave jobs because of unpaid wages or abusive conditions,' noted a Gulf labour rights researcher. 'Penalising them for exercising that choice perpetuates the problem.'

MOHRE has attempted to soften the edges by offering a grievance mechanism — workers can contest the ban by filing a request through the ministry's digital platform. But navigating UAE bureaucracy from a position of vulnerability, often without legal representation, remains a formidable challenge.

What to Watch:

The updated rules take effect immediately. Indian workers in the UAE considering a job switch should ensure their contract terms are fully satisfied and notice periods honoured. The Indian Embassy in Abu Dhabi has previously advised workers to document all employment communications — advice that is now more relevant than ever.
nri_angle: 3.5 million Indians in the UAE are directly affected by these rules; blue-collar and mid-level Indian workers face disproportionate impact from the ban provisions
